claim: Biofilms are spatially organized communities of microorganisms embedded in a self-produced organic matrix.
source: Biofilms are spatially organized communities of microorganisms embedded in a self-produced organic matrix, conferring to the population emerging properties such as an increased tolerance to the action of antimicrobials.
evidence: This is a definitional statement about biofilms that is directly stated in the abstract.

claim: Biofilms confer to the population emerging properties such as an increased tolerance to the action of antimicrobials.
source: Biofilms are spatially organized communities of microorganisms embedded in a self-produced organic matrix, conferring to the population emerging properties such as an increased tolerance to the action of antimicrobials.
evidence: This statement is supported by established scientific knowledge about biofilm properties.

claim: Some bacilli are able to swim in the exogenous matrix of pathogenic biofilms.
source: It was shown that some bacilli were able to swim in the exogenous matrix of pathogenic biofilms and to counterbalance these properties.
evidence: This claim is supported by prior research as indicated by the passive voice 'it was shown'.

claim: Swimming bacteria can deliver antimicrobial agents in situ.
source: Swimming bacteria can deliver antimicrobial agents in situ, or potentiate the activity of antimicrobial by creating a transient vascularization network in the matrix.

claim: Swimming bacteria can potentiate the activity of antimicrobial by creating a transient vascularization network in the matrix.
source: Swimming bacteria can deliver antimicrobial agents in situ, or potentiate the activity of antimicrobial by creating a transient vascularization network in the matrix.

claim: Biofilm is the most abundant mode of life of bacteria and archaea on earth.
source: Biofilm is the most abundant mode of life of bacteria and archaea on earth (Flemming and Wuertz, 2019; Flemming et al., 2016b).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Flemming and Wuertz, 2019 and Flemming et al., 2016b.

claim: Biofilms are composed of spatially organized communities of microorganisms embedded in a self-produced extracellular polymeric substances (EPS) matrix.
source: They are composed of spatially organized communities of microorganisms embedded in a self-produced extracellular polymeric substances (EPS) matrix.

claim: EPS are typically forming a gel composed of a heterogenous mixture of water, polysaccharides, proteins, and DNA.
source: EPS are typically forming a gel composed of a heterogenous mixture of water, polysaccharides, proteins, and DNA (Flemming et al., 2016a).
evidence: This claim about EPS composition is supported by citation to Flemming et al., 2016a.

claim: The biofilm mode of life confers to the inhabitant microbial community strong ecological advantages such as resistance to mechanical or chemical stresses.
source: The biofilm mode of life confers to the inhabitant microbial community strong ecological advantages such as resistance to mechanical or chemical stresses (Bridier et al., 2011) so that conventional antimicrobial treatments remain poorly efficient against biofilms (Bridier et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Bridier et al., 2011.

claim: Conventional antimicrobial treatments remain poorly efficient against biofilms.

claim: Different mechanisms were invoked such as molecular diffusion-reaction limitations in the biofilm matrix and the cell type diversification associated with stratified local microenvironments.
source: Different mechanisms were invoked such as molecular diffusion-reaction limitations in the biofilm matrix and the cell type diversification associated with stratified local microenvironments (Bridier et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim about mechanisms of biofilm resistance is supported by citation to Bridier et al., 2017.

claim: It was estimated that the biofilm mode of life is involved in 80% of human infection.
source: Indeed, it was estimated that the biofilm mode of life is involved in 80% of human infection and usual chemical control leads to serious environmental issues (Bridier et al., 2011).
evidence: This statistical claim is supported by citation to Bridier et al., 2011.

claim: Motile bacteria have been observed in host biofilms formed by exogenous bacterial species.
source: Motile bacteria have been observed in host biofilms formed by exogenous bacterial species (Houry et al., 2012; Li et al., 2014; Piard et al., 2016; Flemming et al., 2016a).
evidence: This observation is supported by multiple citations: Houry et al., 2012; Li et al., 2014; Piard et al., 2016; Flemming et al., 2016a.

claim: Bacterial swimmers are able to penetrate the dense population of host bacteria and to find their way in the interlace of EPS.
source: These bacterial swimmers are able to penetrate the dense population of host bacteria and to find their way in the interlace of EPS.

claim: Bacterial swimmers leave behind them a trace in the biofilm structure, that is a zone of extracellular matrix free of host bacteria.
source: Doing so, they visit the 3D structure of the biofilm, leaving behind them a trace in the biofilm structure, that is a zone of extracellular matrix free of host bacteria (Figure 1a and Appendix 1—figure 3).

claim: Bacterial swimmers dig a network of capillars in the biofilm, enhancing the diffusivity of large molecules.
source: Hence, bacterial swimmers are digging a network of capillars in the biofilm, enhancing the diffusivity of large molecules (Houry et al., 2012), allowing the transport of biocide at the heart of the biofilm, reducing islands of living cells.

claim: B. sphaericus is the longest bacteria by a factor of approximately 1.5 compared to B. pumilus and B. cereus.
